Pending further investigation regulatory action should be undertaken.Manuscript Keywords 7-hydroxymitragynine; 7-OH, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl; kratom; opioid 1.0 Background Kratom, a psychoactive botanical taken for centuries in Southeast Asia, is increasingly usedAuthor in the West for its mild stimulatory and euphoric effects (Cinosi et al. 2015; Smith et al. 2023; Smith, Panlilio, Feldman, et al. 2024). Mitragynine, kratom’s most abundant alkaloid that acts at adrenergic, opioid, dopamine, and serotonin receptors, may be responsible for many of kratom’s neuropsychiatric effects. (León et al. 2021; Obeng et al. 2022; Ponglux et al. 1994). The chemical 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) is not present in fresh kratom leavesManuscript but is an artifact of the drying process (Zhang et al. 2022, Smith, et al. 2024; Sharma, 2025); it is also formed by oxidation of mitragynine by hepatic and intestinal cytochromes. The binding affinity of 7-OH at the mu-opioid receptor (MOR) is 10-22 greater than morphine; 7-OH is further metabolized in humans to mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MP), a chemical nearly as potent as fentanyl (Chakraborty et al. 2021; Kamble et al. 2020; Kruegel et al. 2016; 2019; Qu et al. 2023). Because 7-OH and MP are not found in fresh, native kratom leaf (Zarembo et al., 1974) products containing these ingredients manufactured through conversion of mitragynine can be considered semi-synthetic derivatives of mitragynine. TheAuthor safety of 7-OH and MP in humans is unstudied. Kratom products sold in the West include extracts and isolates, which differ from traditional decoctions made from boiling fresh leaves, a practice that limits the total alkaloids ingestedManuscript per serving (Brown, Lund, and Murch 2017; Grundmann et al. 2023; Singh, Narayanan, and Vicknasingam 2016). Increasing global demand for kratom has coincided with growing diversity of kratom product formulations that include organic extracts, gummies, vapes, liquid shots, or tablets (Smith, Panlilio, Sharma, et al. 2024). In 2023-2024, however, novel semi-synthetic 7-OH and MP products appeared online with the monikers “7-OH,” “7-hydroxy,” or “7” and, in the case of MP, as “pseudo.” These semisynthetic kratom alkaloids are overwhelmingly mislabeled or marketed as “kratom” even though the chemical composition is wholly distinct (Sharma 2025; Smith et al. 2025).Author The emergence of high potency, non-prescription commercial products derived from kratom impels a better understanding of this semi-synthetic market. Therefore, we investigated the online prevalence of 7-OH and MP products; characterized products’ dosing, cost, and formulation; and reviewed marketing claims including references to “kratom.”Manuscript DrugAlcoholDepend. Hill et al. Page 3 2.0 METHODS 2.1 Data CollectionAuthor Between September 2024-February 2025, we monitored online 7-OH and MP marketing content to compile a product database. We identified vendor websites and products through browser searches using keywords “7-hydroxymitragynine,” “7-hydroxy,” “7-OH,” “Mitragynine pseudoindoxyl,” “pseudoindoxyl,” and “pseudo.” We counted products sold inManuscript varying sizes only once to avoid duplications in the database. Alternatively, some websites sold similar products (e.g., drink mix) under different flavors. If these contained slightly different formulations and/or made separate claims, we considered them distinct. 2.2 Product and Marketing Content 2.2.1Productcategorizationwas coded as: “7-OH,” “MP,” or “combination 7-OH and MP.” 2.2.2Productinformationwas obtained by scraping websites for: URL, brand name,Author product name, complete amount (mg) in full package, mg in a single dosing unit, mg in recommended dose/serving, online product description, product images, product cost per package, cost per serving, servings per package, customer reviews, and semi-synthetic substance(s).Manuscript 2.2.3Producttypewas classified: chewable/sublingual tablets, shots, gummies, drink mixes, vape pens, syrups, capsules, food products, sublingual strips, or powders. 2.2.3Productclaimswere roughly classified: “general wellbeing claims,” “functional claims,” or “drug claims” and identified by reading product descriptions across websites and product packaging, including images when available. “Generalwellbeingclaims” were statements linking the semi-synthetic product to beneficial general effects; products were categorized into the following emergent general wellbeing claims: boosting energy,Author increasing focus, improving wellbeing, improving mood, providing relaxation, and workout supplement. General wellbeing claims that we identified were similar, but not always equivalent, to those of a structure/function claim of a dietary supplement as defined by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Borchers, Keen, & Gershwin, 2016). “FunctionalManuscript claims”were statements that linked the product to more specific therapeutic-like outcomes; products were categorized into the emergent functional claims: pain/discomfort relief or management, and stress/anxiety reduction. “Drugclaims”were statements indicating the product conferred some specific therapeutic outcome, such as stimulatory or opioid activity. Note that this claim is not isomorphic with disease claims, which dietary supplements are not permitted to make. We want to emphasize that our categorizations for product claims are not rigid and that, depending on specific marketing language, could correspond to one or more products claims. As such, our three types of “claims” provide only a crude method forAuthor categorizing the statements made online for novel 7-OH and MP marketing. Manuscript DrugAlcoholDepend. Hill et al. Page 4 2.3 Data Analysis Quantitative analyses were done using Excel with findings summarized descriptively. We abstracted and present illustrative quotes but have removed brand names. These appear in theAuthor full Supplement 1 database; we strongly encourage readers to view this material. 3.0 RESULTS We identified 304 products: 82.2% sold as 7-OH, 14.5% as combination 7-OH-MP, andManuscript 3.3% as MP. Note that text segments quoted in the results may exemplify more than one product claim type (each type was coded separately and quantified). 3.1 Product Type, Dosage, Claims, and Reviews Table 1 shows marketed semi-synthetic products by type. Chewable/sublingual tablets were the most common (60.2%), followed by shots (20.7%). Websites stressed the ease of using semi-synthetics compared to kratom. For instance, a 7-OH chewable tablet is marketed asAuthor follows: “The chewable format is designed for convenience, allowing you to simply chew a tablet and savor the berry flavor. This eliminates the need for mixing or preparation… The compact size of each tablet makes them portable and perfectManuscript for on-the-go use, so you can carry them in your bag or pocket and take them whenever needed.” In this way, many websites marketed semi-synthetics as consumer-friendly formulations while highlighting that kratom products required effort to prepare. Table 1 summarizes products’ characteristics and websites and/or packaging that made specific claims or misleadingly presented their product as kratom. Most (73.4%) of products made what we considered to be generalwellbeingclaims, the most common being increasedAuthor focus (58.2%), provides relaxation (46.7%), or boosts energy (39.5%). Products sold as 7-OH had a greater proportion of effect claims (76.8%) than MP (50.0%) or combination products (59.1%). Emblematic of the effect claims is one 7-OH vendor’s description of the benefits customers might expect:Manuscript “Enhanced Relaxation, Focus, Energy Motivation, Mood Elevation, Body Buzz, Euphoria, Discomfort Suppression, Apprehension Relief, Feeling Present, Stimulation, Arousal, Social Lubrication” Functionalclaimswere made by 37.8% of labels or websites, generally related to pain relief (26.3%) stress/anxiety reduction (21.4%) effects. One 7-OH product touted: “Each tablet contains 15mg of 7-Hydroxymitragynine, a compound renowned forAuthor its strong analgesic and mood-enhancing properties. This makes ‘[Brand] Kratom Chewable Tablets’ an ideal choice for those seeking quick relief from pain, anxiety, or stress, as well as those looking to improve their overall sense of well-being.” Some branded their products to imply curative powers associated with prescriptions. One 7-OH vendor stated: “Every pouch includes four expertly pressed classic extract tablets. These tabletsAuthor are scored down the center for easy dosing and contain two servings total. Lastly, while some products had many customer reviews (up to 143Manuscript for 7-OH), most had zero or few reviews. 4.0 DISCUSSION We identified widespread online marketing of semi-synthetic products containing ingredients which, if accurate, have high MOR binding affinity. We identified that 7-OH as the most common constituent of commercial semi-synthetic products. The difficulty and expense of isolating 7-OH from kratom leaves, but also the sheer amount of activeAuthor ingredient, strongly suggests that these semi-synthetic products are manufactured in a laboratory from purified mitragynine. The chemical processes used to make 7-OH also likely places consumers at risk for inadvertent exposure to toxicity from synthetic reagents and reaction by-products. Novel 7-OH products, therefore, carry fundamentally different risksManuscript than those presented by the kratom market that existed in the US for nearly 20 years (Boyer et al. 2008; Smith et al. 2022). The trend toward increasingly potent semi-synthetic chemicals based upon kratom alkaloids is concerning. Product descriptions frequently hinted at neuropsychiatric opioidergic effects with terms such as “buzz” or “euphoria” coupled with brand names that evoke opioids (e.g., Roxy, Opia, Hydroxie, Perks). Consumers may not appreciate that 7-OH products may induce tolerance and withdrawal symptoms if used regularly, and can, for some, includeAuthor risks for developing addiction. In some respects, the widespread availability of these semi-synthetic alkaloids is reminiscent of internet ‘pharmacies’ that sold oxycodone and other opioids in the 2000s without prescription. Just as the online pharmacies once did, online 7-OH vendors may useManuscript discreet packaging and direct-to-home shipping practices to obviate state laws intended to protect consumers. Whereas kratom products have been adulterated with hydrocodone and morphine (LeSaint et al., 2022), the potency of semi-synthetic kratom alkaloids may obviate the need for adulteration with opioids. Marketing of these products poses problems. First, labeling 7-OH and MP products as “kratom” misleads consumers who intend to use a low-potency botanical supplement but instead ingest a high-potency opioid. Second, websites may persuade consumersAuthor that 7-OH and MP formulations are chemically pure and consistently manufactured; however, online photographs from some manufacturers themselves show several vials of powdered 7-OH, each a different shade in color that indicates differences in composition and purity. Inconsistencies in manufacturing and non-adherence to good manufacturingManuscript practices likely lead to variation in dose and composition of products, which, due to the DrugAlcoholDepend. Finally, the marketing material for some formulations (e.g., sublingual tablets) ignore their products’ increased bioavailability which, when coupled with relatively shorter duration of actionAuthor of 7-OH, heightens the risk of dependence or addiction (Maxwell et al. 2021; Sharma 2025). We conclude that the widespread availability of these semi-synthetics represents an unrecognized but growing public health threat Our methodology has limitations. Products sold in brick-and-mortar stores were notManuscript included in this sample, although the location of sales would not affect the pharmacology under discussion (Hemby et al. 2019). We did not chemically analyze products or interview consumers; this work, however, is underway and beyond the scope of this exploratory project. We are confident that health risks of 7-OH and MG are real, as forensic toxicologists have identified 7-OH in postmortem samples (Osawa and Johnson 2025).
